newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank was target of massive fraud - newsletter.
newsitem.headline: French bank was target of massive fraud - newsletter.

text.p: The rescue vehicle set up to dispose of dud assets belonging to Credit Lyonnais alleged in an internal newsletter that the French state-owned bank was the target of massive fraud before 1993.

"The further the CDR teams advance, thanks to their audits...one thing becomes clear -- the existence of an organised fraud until 1993," the state-backed holding company Consortium de Realisation alleged in the document.
The CDR was set up in 1995 to sell off nearly 200 million francs of Credit Lyonnais' bad assets under a state rescue of the bank.

The CDR said the alleged fraud involved seven former units of Credit Lyonnais -- including Altus Finance, SDBO, SAGA and Colbert -- not the parent bank -- and that the cost of "this financial apocalypse" was above figures recently mentioned.

The CDR told a parliamentary commission in March it expected the cost of its sell-off operation to total 102 billion francs over a number of years to 2014 but that did not include carrying costs of the assets, expected to be around 30 billion francs.
The CDR said the fraud amounted to a "veritable looting, often concealed by false balance sheets," and that the former management was too obliging.

Credit Lyonnais almost collapsed in the early 1990s after an ill-fated expansion binge which briefly made it the biggest bank outside Japan. The bank, which has received massive state handouts, could be privatised as early as this year.
The strongly worded document, dated May 1997, was addressed to "all those who work for the sucessful completion of (CDR's) mission".

It was intended as a "morale-boosting exercise for the troops in face of attacks from various quarters" over the CDR's performance, a CDR spokesman said without specifying the origin of the the attacks.
He said there was nothing new in the newsletter. CDR chairman Michel Rouger had made similar comments to a parliamentary committee investigating the banking scandal, he said.
Some 75 legal proceedings are underway involving the affair, with more expected to come.
Last year, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said he wanted to bring senior managers to justice for failing to keep control of subsidiaries during the expansion spree.
Credit Lyonnais, meanwhile, stressed that the problems raised by the CDR involved the "old Credit Lyonnais".

"People must distinguish between the Credit Lyonnais of today which is on the road to recovery and the Credit Lyonnais of the past. These problems involve (Credit Lyonnais) subsidiaries before 1993," said a spokesman for the bank.
